newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, NATO start long, hard road to agreement.
newsitem.headline: Russia, NATO start long, hard road to agreement.

text.p: Russia and NATO say they have started down a long and winding road towards agreement on a new relationship, despite failing to settle differences over the Western alliance's enlargement plans.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov met for five hours at an official residence outside Moscow on Monday but they agreed only that negotiations would continue and that they would be hard.
"The meeting was useful although, of course, there are different approaches on a range of questions," a brief Russian foreign ministry statement said.

Officials in Brussels, where NATO has its headquarters, agreed that the two sides remained far apart. "We have a long way to go, we are very far apart on a number of issues," said one senior official.

Relations are soured by disagreement over NATO's plans to take in former Soviet bloc countries from eastern and central Europe. Moscow says such expansion into the former Soviet bloc would threaten its security and cause new divisions in Europe.
Little time remains for reaching an understanding before a July summit in Madrid at which NATO is expected to issue invitations to the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.
But despite the time pressure and a lack of clear progress at Monday's talks, officials in Moscow and Brussels dismissed talk of failure.
"A timetable was set out for more work in the weeks ahead," a Russian foreign ministry source told Interfax mews agency. "In no way can you call it (the meeting) a failure."
President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said: "It is just the first round...in mutual relations between Russia and NATO."
Officials in Brussels also hailed Monday's meeting.
"It was positive, at least now the negotiation process has been launched," a Western ambassador said.
He said Solana had succeeded in getting across the message that the alliance wanted to deal and had won an agreement to talk again in the near future although no date was set.
The officials in Brussels said Solana had also presented detailed proposals on a permanent consultative mechanism on offer to help Russia accept the alliance's expansion.
"We wanted to show we had specific proposals, not just ideas. We think Primakov was impressed we had done our homework," said one senior official.
The official said Solana had made clear that any deal with Russia on a charter encompassing all aspects of a new relationship would not be a "consolation prize" for enlargement.
NATO says the Madrid summit will go ahead as planned even if talks with Russia do not bear fruit by then.

The dispute poses problems for Yeltsin. He does not want to alienate Russia's Western partners or risk new global tensions, but he will face fierce criticism by his political rivals if he fails to win concessions before NATO enlargement goes ahead.

Any discontent over his handling of NATO could also increase demands for him to step down on health grounds following his heart problems last year and the pneumonia which forced him to spend 12 says in hospital before his release on Monday.
